question: Is there a clear decentralised procedure for approvals of each level of plans? >:< Does the law mandate that the metropolitan/regional plan be approved by the state government?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Yes, in our reading. Under Gujarat law, the plan for a metropolitan area (the development plan made under the Gujarat Metropolitan Planning Committees Act, 2008, or MPC Act) gets legal force only when the State Government sanctions it. Section 10A was added to the MPC Act by Gujarat Act No. 14 of 2019. It lets the State Government sanction the draft plan, refuse it, or send it back. Only the version the State sanctions becomes the 'final development plan'. The State then notifies when it comes into force, and from that date it binds all authorities in the metropolitan area. The provision says 'may', but that word only lists the State's choices. No other body can approve the plan and no other route makes it final. So State approval is in effect compulsory for the metropolitan plan to have legal effect. The Surat Metropolitan Planning Committee prepares the plan, or an authorised officer does. Surat Municipal Corporation, the city government, does not approve it. | EVIDENCE: (1) MPC Act s.10A(1)-(3), added by clause 9 of Gujarat Act 14 of 2019 (Gazette Ex. 19-08-2019, reproduced in ULG-01 p.97): the State may 'sanction or refuse to sanction the draft development plan... or (b) return the draft development plan to the metropolitan planning committee... for modifying the plan'. s.10A(2): 'The sanction accorded under clause (a)... shall be called the final development plan'. s.10A(3): the final plan is 'binding on the concerned all authorities functioning in the metropolit

(3) A final development plan which has come into force shall be binding on the concerned all authorities functioning in the metropolitan area.

comments:
I agree with the Step 2 answer: YES. This is the sub-question (SQ) worth 3.33: does the law require the State Government to approve the metropolitan/regional plan?

(1) What the law says. Under the Gujarat MPC Act s.10A(1), as inserted in 2019, the State Government receives the draft development plan from the Metropolitan Planning Committee (MPC). It may then (a) sanction it, refuse it, or sanction it with changes, or (b) send it back to the MPC for changes. Under s.10A(2), only the plan the State sanctions becomes the 'final development plan', and it comes into force on a date the State notifies. Under s.10A(3), that final plan binds all authorities in the metropolitan area. Under s.10B, any change to the final plan also needs State sanction. Under s.10C, the MPC must follow State directions, and the State's decision on any dispute is final. So no plan can become final or binding without State sanction.

(2) The word 'may'. The verb in s.10A(1) is 'may', but it lists the State's choices: sanction, refuse or return. It does not create another way for the plan to become final. I read State approval as a legal requirement for the plan to take effect. A reviewer should confirm this reading.

I scored NO with low confidence. A reviewer should confirm it before it stands.

**The plan.** ULG-09 is the Economic Master Plan for the Surat Economic Region. NITI Aayog prepared it, dated September 2024, with a vision to 2047. It is a six-district regional plan and says its framework is 'indicative'.

**What I checked for a role given to Surat Municipal Corporation (SMC) or urban local bodies (ULBs).** On top of the Step 2 passages, I ran targeted searches across the EMP:
- Executive summary s.7: three-tier framework of the Empowered Group of Ministers (EGM), the State High Power Steering Committee (SHPSC) and the proposed regional authority, SREDA. SMC has no tier of its own.
- Chapter 10.1:
  - SREDA is the responsible entity, and ULBs only have 'official representation' on it.
  - Implementation duties go to the G-Hub Crack Unit (coordination and KPI monitoring), a tourism body (DMO) and a Project Management Unit (structuring and financing). None of these is SMC.
- Chapter 10.2: monitoring names 'State Governments and Development Authorities'. ULBs are not named.
- Annexure I: the SMC Municipal Commissioner, a Deputy Municipal Commissioner, the City Engineer and the Chief Town Planner sit on the state-chaired Steering Committee and the G-Hub Crack Unit, which the Urban Development and Urban Housing Department chairs. I treated this as individual officers on state bodies, not a role assigned to the ULG.
- Annexure IV (chemicals): GIDC and iNDEXTb are named. 'ICCC of Surat' (the Integrated Command and Control Centre) is to be the nodal monitoring entity for environmental compliance.
  - Elsewhere the plan calls it the 'ICCC of Surat Smart City' and never says SMC owns it.
  - The task is environmental compliance, not economic targets.
- Annexure VII (tourism): implementing agencies are tagged on each project, namely GMB, State Tourism Department, Development Authority, Forest Department, DRDA and private parties. None is SMC or a ULB.
- Annexure VIII (agriculture): projects list locations, with no ULG named.
- s.8.1: green-building guidelines 'can be ... implemented by Local Authorities'. This is a discretionary, generic climate measure that names no ULG.
- Every other SMC mention I found is descriptive, such as a groundwater statistic or a bibliography entry.

- The read tool returns only the most relevant passages, so I could not read every page word for word. In particular, I did not fully see the sector chapters 5-9 or the real-estate and other annexures. A page-by-page check for any project naming SMC as implementing or financing agency would make this affirmative absence conclusive.
- Please confirm two judgements:

  - (b) The Surat ICCC monitoring role is not attributable to SMC as given in the plan.
- I did not check UPD26a/b, so it is unconfirmed that this regional EMP is the 'city Economic Vision Plan' the question means.
- ULG-06 (SUDA Development Plan 2035) is a statutory land-use plan by the Surat Urban Development Authority, not an economic vision plan.
- The Step 2 answer left this undetermined. My extra reads found no SMC assignment, and they found agency-tagged project lists that leave SMC out.

Part 1 (approval authority at each level) = YES, with a caveat:

- The State sanctions or refuses the metropolitan final development plan, and sanctions variations to it, under MPC Act ss.10A-10B, inserted by the 2019 amendment (ULG-01, PRS copy).

Part 2 (rejection/variance process) = YES, in law:
- CGDCR p.58: Competent Authority 'may grant or refuse'. 'Reasons for rejection of application shall be communicated to the applicant.' Permission is granted only when the proposal complies.
- CGDCR p.60: revalidation is scrutinised 'in context of proposals of Development Plan'.
- GTPUD s.49(1)(b) proviso (2017): permission 'shall be in accordance with the Draft Town Planning Scheme'.
- MPC Act s.10B: State variation procedure for the development plan (objections invited, MPC consulted).
- Caveat: s.10B uses 'may sanction'. It is a procedure for varying the plan, not a project-level variance procedure.

Checked, with nothing found: ULG-01, ULG-03, ULG-04 (Rule 53 only allows inspection of TP schemes), ULG-05, ULG-06, ULG-07, ULG-09, ULG-10 and ULG-13. ULG-12 is a single TP scheme map, not a registry. Not finding a website here is a VERIFICATION-LIMIT, not proof that no registry exists, so this cannot be marked NO.

Part 4 (public disclosure) = blank. CGDCR Common Protocol item 4 (p.61) creates a legal duty: the Competent Authority 'must display the grant of permission or rejection or suspension online in public domain'. But there is no evidence that SMC or SUDA actually publishes approvals, denials and variances. A legal mandate is not proof of practice. VERIFICATION-LIMIT.

A person should:
1. Confirm which body is the Competent Authority within SMC limits and which in the SUDA area.
2. Capture dated screenshots of any SMC/SUDA online building-permission portal that shows a project registry and lists of approvals and rejections, then complete parts 3 and 4.

I scored this as a question about the law, following the Detailed Methodology ('Check the applicable T&CP Act or the allied Act, and Municipal Act for provisions'). The question bank tags it as 'Implementation', but the Citation Sheet has no dated evidence of inspections actually happening in Surat. A reviewer should confirm that the law-based reading is intended. If practice evidence is required, these inputs should be left blank.

All three aspects are met, so the band is 5/5.

(1) Authority to inspect:
- ULG-05 (CGDCR 2017, p.64): 'the Competent Authority reserves the right to inspect such buildings at any time during the Period of Construction without giving prior notice', and owners 'shall Permit authorized officers ... to enter'.
- I checked this against ULG-13, the Municipal Act's Chapter XV as published by SMC. The Step 2 answer had not read it. s.259: 'The Commissioner may at any time during the erection of a building ... make an inspection thereof, without giving previous notice'.
- s.261 allows suspect work to be cut into and laid open for inspection.

(2) Stage-wise monitoring:
- ULG-05 says buildings 'shall be subject to periodic inspection ... during construction'.
- Form 10 is the notice of commencement. Under Reg 5.5.3, Schedule 13 and Form 11, the professionals must notify progress and certify compliance at basement slab, plinth, ground floor, middle storey and last storey.
- On a progress notice, the authority has a duty, 'if found necessary', to check deviation from the sanctioned plan within 7 days.
- Protocol item 10 requires e-intimation at plinth and later stages. Item 12 requires inspection at different stages.
- Reg 6.1: the authority 'shall undertake final inspection' within 21 days of the completion notice.
- Caveat: stage reporting is mainly the builder's duty, and the authority checks 'if found necessary'. Still, the regulations set up a mandatory stage-wise monitoring system with commencement, plinth, intermediate and completion stages, which is what the rubric asks for.

(3) Notice and stop-work power:
- ULG-05 p.41: the Competent Authority 'may, by a written notice, require the person undertaking construction of the building to stop the same forthwith'. It 'shall' take action including demolition and directions for alteration, and may seal the site with police help.
- The Municipal Act (ULG-13 / ULG-03) gives the same powers: s.260 (show-cause notice), s.262 (notice of contravention during erection) and s.267(1) (notice to 'stop the same forthwith').
- ULG-04, the 1979 Rules, adds a stop-work notice.
- These stop-work powers use 'may'. The rubric only asks whether the power exists.

Period covered:
- CGDCR as notified on 12.10.2017; I did not check later amendments. The copy is hosted by AUDA, but the instrument is a statewide Government of Gujarat notification.
- ULG-13 is an undated SMC copy of the Act; ULG-03 is the text as modified to 30.11.2017.
- I did not read the enforcement sections of the Town Planning Act 1976 (ULG-01). They are not needed, because every input is already met.

I left the count blank. The question tests the planning Act, the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 (GTPUDA). The Citation Sheet copy of it (ULG-01, PRS) has no readable text for the principal Act, which should be on pages 2-86. Only the amendment Acts appended to it can be read. So the Act's own penal sections cannot be mapped head by head. A partial count of 2-3 would push the answer to 'No', and that needs affirmative absence, which I cannot show. I agree with Step 2 that the score should stay blank, but I found more evidence than Step 2 did.

What the Citation Sheet does show, by head:

(a) Head 5, work without permission: covered.
- CGDCR 2017 (ULG-05, p.41), for development started without permission: 'Such development will be considered unauthorised and over and above the Development Permission Scrutiny fees as leviable and stipulated in Schedule 3, penalty shall be charged as per Schedule 6.' The same regulation lets the authority demolish unauthorised works, seal the building unit and use police help.
- GTPUD Rules 1979, r.11 and Form E (ULG-04): for breaches of s.27/28/29, s.34 and s.49, the authority 'shall serve a notice in writing upon the person contravening' requiring removal, alteration or demolition, stopping of work, ending of use or restoration of the land.

(b) Head 1b, permitted use / change of use: covered. CGDCR Schedule 16 (quoted above) sets a fine of four times the scrutiny fee for unauthorised use of a building.

(c) Head 6, urban design / signage: only partly. CGDCR Schedule 18 says the authority 'may also decide penalty norms for non-compliance of Regulations specified for Advertising Display Structures'. That is 'may' and leaves the penalty to be set later, so I did not count it.

(d) Encroachment / plan contravention, Local Area Plans only: GTPUDA s.76A(8), added by Act 22 of 2017 (ULG-01), says the authority 'shall' remove buildings that contravene a Local Area Plan and recover the costs.

(e) Town Planning schemes: Form L (r.34, s.69 GTPUDA) allows removal of works that contravene a scheme.

(f) The Municipal Act (GPMC Act 1949, ULG-03) also has penal provisions:
- s.392 and Appendix II give fines for contravening listed sections, plus daily fines for continuing offences.
- A provision on p.197 lets the Magistrate order removal of a building or discontinuance of use after conviction.
- ULG-13 (Chapter XV, Building Regulations) has s.261, 262, 267 and 268: enforcement against unlawful building work and unlawful occupation.
This is the Municipal Act, not the planning Act the methodology names. I did not map its Appendix II items to the heads, because I could not read the full table.

Not found in what I could read: specific penalties for setbacks, height, FSI, parking, heritage, environment, fire and other building-code items, NOC breaches (fire, water, electricity, pollution, solid waste, airport height), or general encroachment.

A person needs to:
(i) get a readable official text of GTPUDA 1976 and check its penalty and unauthorised-development sections (around s.35-36 and the offences chapter);
(ii) read CGDCR Schedule 6 and the enforcement regulations 2.12 and 6.1.5 in full;
(iii) decide whether removal and stop-use orders count as 'penal provisions';
(iv) decide whether CGDCR and GPMC provisions count, given that the methodology says 'T&CP Act'.

Periods covered: GTPUDA as amended up to Act 14 of 2019; GTPUD Rules 1979 (SUDA copy); CGDCR notified 12 Oct 2017; GPMC Act as modified up to 30 Nov 2017.
